analysis.one_liner: Bans self-bonding so coal companies must post real money to pay for cleaning up their mines.
analysis.headline: The bill to end self-bonding for coal mine cleanup never received a committee vote in the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When a coal company goes bankrupt, the law requires it to restore the mined land. Under "self-bonding," a company could simply promise it had the money, with no outside guarantee — so if it went bankrupt, taxpayers footed the cleanup bill. This bill would have banned new self-bonds, required existing ones to be replaced with surety or collateral bonds, barred using the coal mine itself as collateral, and tightened rules on the bonding companies, so the cost of cleanup stays with the industry that made the mess [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would no longer be on the hook when a self-bonded coal company goes bankrupt; and nearby communities, who would see mined land actually restored rather than abandoned with the cleanup debt unpaid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near coal mines

how_it_helps.text: Bars federal and state regulators from accepting new self-bonds, so cleanup obligations must be backed by a third-party surety or real collateral.
Forces existing self-bonds and corporate surety bonds to be converted to stronger bonds, with rules limiting surety-bond concentration and requiring minimum collateralization.
Prohibits counting the coal mine itself as collateral — the very asset that becomes worthless when a company fails — and allows executive compensation to count toward bonding.

analysis.who_pays: Coal companies that used self-bonding to avoid paying for real financial assurance; they would have had to buy surety bonds or post collateral, a real cost for weaker firms.

drawbacks.text: Requiring surety or collateral bonds raises the cost of operating a coal mine, which in coal-dependent regions was framed as a burden on an already struggling industry and its workers.
Because existing self-bonds only had to be replaced at permit renewal or major modification, some companies could have kept operating under old self-bonds for years after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — ending a practice that lets insolvent coal companies leave reclamation bills with taxpayers — is real and the costs fall mainly on the companies and surety industry that created the risk. The main trade-off acknowledged even by supporters of bonding reform is that stricter bonding requirements raise mining costs, which could push marginal operations toward bankruptcy and abandonment, though the bill addresses this by requiring collateral that cannot simply be the mine itself. The bill was narrow and targeted, not a broad mining ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced; no committee vote, no floor vote, and the Congress ended with the bill dead in committee.

narrative.text: Introduced March 30, 2017, by Senator Cantwell and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day.
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies that self-bond kept the ability to promise their own solvency for cleanup, leaving taxpayers to cover the bill when companies fail.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban self-bonding for coal mine reclamation.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote in the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four senators behind the bill were Democrats, and with Republicans controlling the Senate and its committees the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would have ended cheap self-bonding, forcing companies to post real surety or collateral bonds for reclamation, a direct cost to an industry where several large operators had used self-bonding while financially weak.
Converting self-bonds and corporate bonds to surety bonds would have sent more bonding business to surety companies, though subject to new federal rules on collateralization and concentration.
Taxpayers currently absorb reclamation costs when self-bonded companies go bankrupt; the bill would have removed that exposure.
